title: Lamrim: death
hook: death is certain, its time uncertain, only practice helps at that time

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first stair of the lamrim: this precious life, rare as a blind turtle finding the yoke. Did you name one freedom at a red light or a sink of dishes? Today, the next stair. Day one thousand two hundred ninety.

A village asleep in a river valley. Lamps out, doors shut, everyone dreaming about tomorrow's chores. In the night the river rises, and by morning the village is gone. The Dhammapada uses that picture for a person wrapped up in family and possessions, carried off by death before they've looked up. It's not a gentle image. It isn't meant to be. Yesterday the lamrim said this life is precious. Today it adds the other half, the one that gives the first its weight: this precious life is going to end, and nobody has told us when.
screen: `A VILLAGE ASLEEP.` → `THE RIVER RISES IN THE NIGHT.` → `PRECIOUS, AND IT ENDS.`

segments.voice: First, death is certain. The lamrim doesn't ask anyone to dwell on gloom. It asks for something plainer: to notice that no one who was born has stayed. The great teachers died. The Buddha died. Every person in an old photograph is gone or going. None of this is news, and yet the mind manages to live as if it were someone else's news. Second, the time is uncertain. Here's where the teaching bites. A life has no fixed length. Healthy people die suddenly, the old sometimes outlive the young, and the things that keep a body alive, food, a car, a doctor's medicine, can in a bad moment be the things that end it. So tomorrow is not a promise. It's a likely guess. Third, at that time only practice helps. The Dhammapada says that when death seizes someone, sons are no help, nor a father, nor relatives. The lamrim adds wealth and the body itself to the list. You can't bring the house, the savings, the reputation. What goes with you, in this teaching, is the shape your mind has taken: the patience, the kindness, the clarity you actually practiced. Fourth, why this belongs on the staircase. Lamrim teachers put death right after precious human life on purpose. Precious life alone can turn into a reason to relax. Precious life plus an unknown end turns into urgency, the good kind: not panic, but a clear sense of what matters today. Certain and uncertain, held together, sort the important from the merely loud.
screen: `DEATH IS CERTAIN.` · `ITS TIME IS UNCERTAIN.` · `AT THAT TIME, ONLY PRACTICE HELPS.` · `PRECIOUS PLUS UNKNOWN: GOOD URGENCY.` · then, large: `CERTAIN, UNCERTAIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: three minutes of reflection. Let the sit be the start of it. Breathe, and let the body grow still. Say quietly to yourself: this life will end. Let that sit for a few breaths. Then: I don't know when. A few more breaths. Then ask, gently, without pressure: if that's true, what matters today? Don't force an answer. If this feels too heavy right now, simply rest with the breath instead. The bell holds the time.
Lamrim, the next stair: death. Certain that it comes, uncertain when, and at that time only practice helps. Today's word.
Your line: certain, uncertain. Today, before you put off one kind word or one call you've meant to make, remember tomorrow is a guess, and do it now. Day one thousand two hundred ninety.

howItsDone: In lamrim practice, students meditate on death's certainty, the uncertainty of its time, and that only practice helps at death, reflecting on each point in turn during regular meditation sessions.

notes: Dhammapada 287 and 288 are paraphrased, not quoted; confirm the verse numbers and the paraphrases.
The lamrim's further subpoints (three roots, nine reasons) are not counted under the claims rule; the three points are named only as the index hook gives them.
'Healthy people die suddenly, the old sometimes outlive the young' and food/medicine becoming causes of death: common lamrim examples, stated generally; confirm.
The outline asks for three minutes of reflection; the app's sit is two minutes, so the practice frames the sit as the start.
Sensitive topic: the practice offers an opt-out ('if this feels too heavy, rest with the breath'). Keep it.
Original मरणसति (Pali maranasati) is the Pali term, not the Tibetan; confirm it is appropriate here.
Editor: practice no longer mentions 'the outline' aloud; fixed subject-verb agreement ('sort').
